summary: A C string is a char array whose end is marked by the NUL character '\0'. There is no string type and no length stored anywhere, so every library routine walks until it finds the terminator. Mismanaging that terminator or buffer size is behind a large share of C security bugs.

sections.heading: Representation
sections.body: The string "Geeks" occupies 6 bytes: five characters plus the terminator. `strlen` counts characters before the NUL; `sizeof` of the array counts the NUL too.

sections.heading: Array versus literal pointer
sections.body: `char s[] = "hi"` makes a modifiable copy on the stack. `const char *p = "hi"` points at a literal in read-only memory; writing through it is undefined behavior (usually a crash). Declare literal pointers `const` so the compiler catches mistakes.
sections.code:
char a[] = "hi"; a[0] = 'H';        // ok
const char *p = "hi"; /* p[0] = 'H'; */  // UB

sections.heading: Reading strings safely
bullets: `scanf("%s")` stops at whitespace and has no bound: always give a width, `%19s`.
`fgets(buf, sizeof buf, stdin)` reads a whole line including the newline and respects the buffer size.
`gets` was removed in C11 because it cannot be used safely.

sections.heading: <string.h> essentials
bullets: `strcpy(d, s)`, `strcat(d, s)`: unbounded, caller must guarantee space.
`strncpy(d, s, n)`: bounded, but may leave d without a NUL.
`strcmp(a, b)`: <0, 0, >0; use it, never `==`, to compare contents.
`memcpy`, `memmove`, `memset`: raw byte operations (use memmove when ranges overlap).

sections.heading: Typical pitfalls
bullets: Forgetting room for the NUL when allocating: `malloc(strlen(s) + 1)`.
Comparing with `==` compares addresses, not text.
Using a char array that is not terminated.
Off-by-one in loops that copy characters.

sections.body: `snprintf(dst, sizeof dst, "%s", src)` always terminates and truncates safely; BSD `strlcpy` does the same. If you use `strncpy`, set the last byte to NUL yourself.

`char *names[] = {"ann", "bob"}` is an array of pointers to (possibly differently sized) literals. `char names[2][8]` is a block of fixed rows. `main(int argc, char *argv[])` receives the first form, terminated by a NULL pointer.

`strtok` splits in place by writing NULs into the string (and keeps hidden state, so it is not thread-safe; prefer `strtok_r`). `strtol(s, &end, 10)` converts numbers with error detection through `end` and `errno`, unlike `atoi`.
`char` strings in UTF-8 can hold multi-byte characters, so `strlen` counts bytes, not characters. `wchar_t` and `<wchar.h>` provide wide strings; for real Unicode handling use a library such as ICU.

takeaways: A string is a NUL-terminated char array; length is not stored.
Size buffers for the NUL, and bound every read and copy.
Literals are read-only: use const char * or a char array copy.

references.label: Kernighan & Ritchie, The C Programming Language, 2nd ed.
